Marissa / team / Tom —

Quick tech notes (high level) to send to customer. Will follow with a short appendix if they want deeper numbers.

1) Baseline steady-state latency (redwood-1-medium, 8-bit quant, sequence ~300 tokens): p50 ~ 35–60ms, p95 ~ 90–140ms, p99 ~ 200–320ms. These assume continuous batching disabled for streaming routes (we prioritize TTFB over batch token throughput).

2) Scale-up times:
- Cold start from 0 (no warm pool): full model load and GPU allocation typically 3–5 minutes. Service can return errors or queue during this interval depending on route policy.
- Warm pool active: pre-warmed workers with model loaded: provision additional in ~10–30s depending on instance type and queued payloads.
- Burst routing to lightweight variant: immediate (<1s) routing decision; effective latency will be model-dependent (smaller model => faster).

3) Warm-pool sizing guidance for 200 concurrent streaming sessions:
- Streaming sessions are lightweight on compute but sensitive to TTFB. For redwood-1-medium we estimate approximately 1 worker can sustain ~8–12 concurrent streaming sessions with TTFB targets; conservative planning => 18 warm workers to cover 200 concurrent sessions with headroom.

4) Queueing / backpressure behavior:
- We maintain a bounded in-memory request queue per route. TTL is configurable (default 5s). For streaming routes we prioritize creating a streaming connection (TTFB) and begin token emission; long-running token generation is progressively scheduled. If queue TTL expires we return 503 with a retry-after header.
- Option: configure prioritized TTFB routing for auth flows (drop background tasks to keep TTFB SLO).

5) Pilot / canary proposal (technical):
- Pre-provision 20 warm workers (covers expected concurrency with headroom).
- Run a 7-day canary with staged ramp: 0% -> 1% -> 5% -> 10% traffic over controlled windows, with synthetic load spikes to validate bursts.
- Acceptance: sustained p95 <= 120ms for 95% windows and p99 <= 350ms. If sustained misses occur, fallback to smaller variant + traffic-shaping.

6) Observability hooks we'll enable: per-request latency histograms, time-to-first-byte, streaming chunk latency, token-level cost, and warm-pool utilization. We'll export to your Datadog/Prometheus endpoint.

I can turn this into a 1-page technical note to share with customer. What else do you need?
